utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you could call the case, I think I'll raise it as a preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you call the case, please, and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General Miletic is not present today as you said yesterday he has already forwarded his waiver. Composition today, Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Krgovic, and that's it, I think, and Ms. Tapuskovic. Now, Mr. Haynes. We would like to finish the sitting today because of things that have come up that we have to attend to at 6.15 at the latest. Now, under normal circumstances I would have suggested having two sessions with just one break of 30 minutes. However, I know that you asked for shorter sessions of an hour and 20 minutes each. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll fall in with anything you wish to do to maximise the amount of sitting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. And shall we say that the accused or the -- your client or yourself should you require a break at any time, you will let us know. [French on English channel] I see madam --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that. Can I add one caveat to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your reaction when you walked into this courtroom did not surprise me at all. I had been in court setting up for about 25 or 30 minutes. Several of my colleagues have been in here for not long short of that and the accused himself has been sitting in the chair waiting for you for 10 or 15 minutes, and you will come to realise that the working conditions in this court at the moment are far from ideal. I don't want to be too explicit, but I'm beginning to feel very uncomfortable in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one, Mr. Haynes, and I told my colleagues beforehand that if the temperature is as described to us, unfortunately, I have a condition which cannot tolerate it beyond a certain degree, I feel sick. So I'm telling you this straight and plain that there can come a time unless it comes down, I will have to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was invited by Mr. McCloskey to raise joint concerns. I do wonder whether it's worth fit for purpose at the moment, having been here for 25 or 30 minutes, I'm beginning to feel faint, to be perfectly honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree. It gets hotter the more you sit and given the importance of this sitting, and in what heat does to all of us, I'm sure we could handle it; but I'm not sure that's something that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest opening at least two doors, one at different ends of the courtroom so that the air could circulate and switch off the air-conditioning or the heating system for a while. Because if you switch it off and leave the doors closed, it's going to remain the same. There's too much light, and it will keep the same temperature. As I said, I mean I feel faint after a certain while if it continues like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the idea would be to open this door and then the door of the -- leading to the terrace for a while. That should extract a good part of the heat, but over here, and I don't dispute with security, it's easier said than done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to say I think there may be a security issue. I'm happy to open this door although it leads nowhere as I have explained on the previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we try a bit for a while. Can't that door remain open as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We probably need whoever is in charge of the security today to come in here. That's what I would respectfully suggest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's like being in a sauna here. Was it like this morning as well or what? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is much cooler in that corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, let's start. If you feel uncomfortable, and for that matter, I may feel uncomfortable even before you, then speak up; and we'll see what we will do. But I don't want to keep anyone in this courtroom unduly if the conditions continue to remain like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we'll make a start. Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon when we finished off we were just looking at a few of the events that were going on in the command of the Zvornik Brigade during the morning and the afternoon of the 16th of July, and I trust you will recall that.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now if you don't mind we'll turn our attention to where you were and what you were doing at that time. On the morning of the 16th of July, I think you'd already told us you got up quite early. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I got up before dawn, even before 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I knew, based on the information that I had, that it was possible for combat activities to commence early in the morning in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn our attention, please, to the forces under your command on the morning of the 16th of July. Can you tell us what forces were available to you from the Zvornik Brigade itself?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as clear as possible to start from the most general and then go to the more specific. As usual, the entire Zvornik Brigade was under my command, meaning all the units that made up that brigade. The deployment was slightly unusual, as well as there was some other units of reinforcement and support that had come from elsewhere. In this map behind my back, topographic signs indicate the total tactical and combat situation prevailing on the morning and afternoon of the 16th. By using the technology available to me at the moment, I may try to show you which specific units I have in mind. If we look at this bold red line, and this red spot, this represents the defence line or rather the front line, and that is to say the deployment in the area where the Zvornik Brigade units were; and that is viewing from north towards south-west, that is to say the 1st Battalion, the 5th Battalion, the 2nd Battalion, the 3rd Battalion, the 6th Battalion, the 4th Battalion, and the 7th Battalion. Those were the units entirely deployed on the front line and their level of strength was 100 percent. There were also artillery fire support units and that was actually a mixed artillery division shown by a triangle that you can see here. There was also a battalion firing squad or rather mortar squad for each battalion in their respective defence area. Each mortar was marked like this, that is to say, everybody battalion had their mortar batteries as their own artillery support. The units that were part of the Zvornik Brigade but whose form of deployment was not in the area of Baljkovica were as follows: The Podrinje detachment of the special forces was in the area west of the command post of the 4th Battalion. They were ready both to act on the front and against the 28th Division. Then there was the company of the military police which was deployed at the command post of the 4th Battalion on the east side. There were also two military police regiments of the East Bosnian Corps where the 4th and the 6th Battalions linked up. In addition to that, there were elements of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the witness to slow down when enumerating all these units, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, you are enumerating a good number of units and you are going a little bit too fast for the interpreters. If could slow down, especially when you are mentioning names or indicating units, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I will do that. I think the last unit on the transcript were two platoons of the East Bosnian Corps deployed where the 4th and the 6th Battalions linked up. There was the Bratunac Brigade company on the south-west position vis-a-vis the battalion command post, then there was an intervention platoon from the 2nd Infantry Battalion also close nearby. On the 13th and the 14th July, two companies were established by Dragan Obrenovic and these two were in the area of Crni Vrh: One company was commanded by Major Jovanovic and the other one was commanded by Mr. Maric. Also, west of these two companies was a MUP detachment from Doboj. On the Parlog-Baljkovica axis and this is the line that I'm just showing, were joint forces of the MUP commanded by Ljubisa Borovcanin including a detachment of the special police from Sekovici and PJP Company from Zvornik. There was also a tank company of the Zvornik Brigade which, for the most part, was deployed along the road Crni Vrh-Memici and also on the Orahovac-Parlog-Baljkovica axis. Those were the forces that on the 16th of July available to me and which I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of manpower, what was the approximate number of men under your command on the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we add to this the entire forces of the Zvornik Brigade in the defence area, the total number of men was over 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the units you've just described to us and pointed out on the map?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of July at dawn, all these units were at these locations that I mentioned with the exception of two platoons from the eastern Bosnia Corps who arrived sometime after 10.00 on that same day, that is to say, on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably my fault, Mr. Pandurevic, a bad question. I was asking you how many men were there in the units that you've described and point out on the map behind you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area that I am circling here is an interesting area in terms of the 16th of July and the combat activities carried out there. Around 2.000 troops were directly under my command in that area on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as to the battalions, how would you describe their positions on the front line facing the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line that I showed you which is marked by a bold red line represents the positions of the Zvornik Brigade that for nearly four years had not been shifted either forwards or backwards. Those were the positions that we soldiers usually say excellently fortified, that is to say communicating trenches were there, shelters were there for both the troops and the equipment. In front of these positions, we had prepared minefields and there were occasional wire obstacles. In other words, the front end of the defence of the Zvornik Brigade was remarkably well fortified, and from the [indiscernible] to the north up to Memici and Spreca river to the west, there was a communicating trench dug out which is actually a canal with the depth of 1.20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday about the work you had done during the 15th of July deploying units. What was the position of the 28th Division by the morning of the 16th of July and how were your units deployed in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 15th, we knew the deployment area of the 28th Division. If you look at the map, what I'm showing you now marked with colour blue and number 28, PD represents the forces of the 28th Division. As you can see, the forces under my command were -- had fully blocked the forces of the 28th Division by pushing them forward from the back and from the flanks and keeping them off the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of your position as commander, how were you able to command these units?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my own observation post -- excuse me -- at such a position which gave me a full view of the battle-field or rather the area where the combat activities were going on. Secondly, there was another observation post of the mixed artillery division in this area here and also in the sector of Memici, the observers adjacent to me were also able to view the entire battle-field and to update me about all the changes. I also had radio communications and also wire communications with certain battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to retrace our steps a little bit to amplify something you said. The mixed artillery division, were its guns, as it were, substantially trained in one direction?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mixed artillery division was made up of different kinds of artillery weapons. It was made up of platoons or batteries, one of them was ZIS 76-millimetre guns of Russian make. It also had a 122-millimetre howitzer battery, 155-millimetre howitzer platoon; one, 152-millimetre howitzer and 120-mortar battery made up of six mortars. Their firing positions and their area of activity was such that all the targets in this area stretching from Memici via Nezuk, Baljkovica, et cetera were within their range and within their zone of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could any or all of that artillery have been targeted upon the forces of the 28th Division on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of these weapons were able of firing at the column of the 28th Division and a smaller number of these weapons needed about half an hour in order to adjust their platform at the firing positions in order to be able to fire efficaciously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was there also available at your disposal, as it were, more mobile artillery within the battalions themselves?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a self-propelled 76-millimetre battery which was also part of the formation division. However, at the time it was deployed in the defence area of the 4th Infantry Battalion, I forgot to mention it earlier. We also had tanks that cannot be categorised as artillery weapons but their calibre was large and those were actually four T-55 tanks and T-34 tanks of 75-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to mention anti-aircraft guns, 20, 30, and 56 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now did any combat commence on the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At about what time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat began at around 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from which direction did it commence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat started from the direction of Nezuk, that is to say, from the 246 Mountain Brigade of the 2nd Corps which happened when the artillery fire started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Two questions: Firstly, how heavy was the shelling?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was heavier than usual. During the war, we managed to repel numerous number of the attacks by the 2nd Corps along that axis. In the past, there were fierce artillery fire when Major Petrovic, the brigade commander was wounded; but on this particular day, I could say that the artillery fire was intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how accurate was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the Muslim forces only knew the exact deployment of our forward defence line, that is to say, the units in the trenches, most of their fire originally and initially was concentrated and focused on these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did it hit your positions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire targeting the forward positions created no consequences for the Zvornik Brigade units because a number of positions were in the woods; and on the other hand, we were well-fortified, we had good shelters and covers; and therefore, they suffered no losses as a result of the artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the artillery fire hit anything else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, the artillery fire was transferred, as we soldiers say, in-depth targeting the general area of Baljkovica, Motovska Kosa and Planici. A number of shells landed at a couple of hundred metres from my forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were there any consequences of that for you or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We suffered losses in terms that we had troops wounded and killed. However, I don't know what kind of injuries caused these losses, whether those were caused by artillery fire or rifle fire. At any rate, one can always see and hear and notice artillery fire; and therefore, one has ample time to find cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where were the forces of the 28th Division in relation to where the artillery fire was falling in the depth?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the 28th Division were deployed as shown in the map closer to Baljkovica, and as a result of the artillery fire from the 2nd Corps, they suffered so-called friendly-fire losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did the artillery fire go on for on the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first strikes lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes, which is a standard feature, and it provided support to infantry. After that, fire was opened at different time intervals and without any particular systematic order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During that period, what did the forces of the 28th Division do so far as you could see or find out?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces under my command that were holding the 28th Division under blockade informed me about minor movements and commotion among the troops of the 28th Division in anticipation of the forces to break through from the front and to link up with them. But there was no organised attack by them on that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the forces of the 2nd Division or the 2nd Corps break your lines?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the defence lines of the 4th, 6th and 7th Battalions remained unchanged and all the troops remained in their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the forces of the 28th Division break out of the blockade? you've described?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, some elements of the 28th Division, whilst moving along the -- as I am showing you on this map -- managed to push the crews of self-propelled guns that were deployed in the area because the soldiers having seen a large group of enemy soldiers abandoned their positions because they were not infantry, and they were not trained to fight with rifles in their hands. So two or three guns were captured by the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long were they in the possession of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for long. As soon as we received reports that elements of the 28th Division were there, we targeted this area with our artillery fire and these self-propelled guns stopped firing back. By the way, the position where these guns were deployed had a planned area of operation and this area of operation was actually the Nezuk sector; that is to say, the forces of the 2nd Corps. Since our forces were in Baljkovica in a depression, it was impossible to fire from these guns at a negative angle. Therefore, initially, they fired mainly towards Parlog and towards the southern part from my IKM where the village of Kuce [phoen] was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we might return to that in a little while. Now, you told us yesterday, and we listened to a recording of your conversation with the opposing commander, Semso Muminovic. We'll come on to some conversations you had with him on the 16th of July, but other than him, was there any other contact between your forces and the enemy on the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to exchange of fire, there were those, but if you are talking about radio contact, at one point, we received reports through surveillance that Semso was trying to get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about personal contact between anybody from within your forces and a member of the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, I think it was between 9.00 and 10.00, Dragan Obrenovic, who was in the area of the command post of the 4th Battalion reported to me through means of -- through the communication devices that an officer from the 28th Division had surrendered to him, that this man was wounded, and that he told them the exact deployment and positions of the 28th Division, the number of troops, the number of men under arms, the number of men without arms, and he described how grave the situation in the 28th Division was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember what that man's name was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his last name was Salihovic, and I can't recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did Dragan Obrenovic do with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He interviewed him, they gave him first-aid, and acting on my orders, they let him go back to the division to convey to them that I would establish contact in order to negotiate with them and allow the column to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was explaining my interim combat report of the 15th yesterday, what I had in my mind at the time was a firm decision to open up the front line and let through the forces of the 28th Division. All I had been waiting for was a suitable moment to do that. This seemed to be an excellent moment providing me with a reason to act in this way. I established contact with Semso Muminovic through our radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About what time of the day was that on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our talks began at around 10.00 in the morning or a few minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how quickly did you reach an agreement that morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we reached an agreement relatively quickly, but we needed time for the results of our agreement to be conveyed to all the units on the ground. So this all went on until a little after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you receive the history that the man called Salihovic had given to Dragan Obrenovic, in other words how was it told to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from Dragan Obrenovic in the I have just described. I assumed that the situation in the 20th Division had to be grave, but I had had no idea it was as grave as represented by Mr. Salihovic in his conversation with Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where was Obrenovic when he told you this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the immediate vicinity of the command post of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you tell him to do at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him when he let that man go back or rather once he had let the man go back, he should organise his own evacuation and the evacuation of part of the men who were with him to the point where the 4th and 6th Battalion joined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you tell him to do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to my decision to enter into negotiations and open up a corridor for the passage of the 28th Division, I knew that they would concentrate around the command post and that, in any case, I had to be prepared for possible artillery fire if something went wrong. And that therefore, I had to evacuate Obrenovic from there in order to establish a so-called safe area for artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were the guns of your artillery division repositioned during the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, only one platoon of 105-millimetre howitzers was transferred or repositioned, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you use your artillery during the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my artillery fired on the forces of the 2nd Corps which were attacking from the front line. They were acting -- they were doing so-called barrage fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you use your artillery on the forces of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, the howitzer platoon of the 4th Battalion and probably the 6th fired with their mortars, but later on the artillery of the mixed artillery unit did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I did not issue such an order. I wanted to save as many lives as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What agreement did you reach with Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that soldiers from the 4th Battalion from three trenches should be moved thus opening up a corridor several hundred metres wide. That soldiers from his brigade and my soldiers should be in direct contact, and that the column of the 28th Division was being invited and called upon and directed to pass through that corridor. We knew the name of the feature, it was a small place called Resnik and Zuta Zemlja. They passed along that axis. Let me add that part of the agreement was that some of the soldiers from the 2nd Corps should enter in the direction of Baljkovica and assist in the evacuation of the wounded and the ill who were in the column of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was there anything you asked for in return as part of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the agreement was reached, when we had agreed on every detail, I had no counter-requests to make. Later on, I heard that a soldier named Tesic had been taken prisoner, and I asked him to be sent back, to be exchanged. At the insistence of some members of the MUP, I also asked for an exchange because Mr. Jankovic had been captured previously and was held by Semso Muminovic, so I asked for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How was the agreement put into effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was implemented in full at around 1300 or 1400 hours. Parts of the 28th Division were already passing through the corridor and going off in the direction of Nezuk. Their passage continued until nightfall. It was supervised by both sides. We had agreed that if either side violated the agreement one-sidedly, the other side could open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What preceded the actual opening of the lines?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A complete cessation of hostilities, informing all the units on the ground and the beginning of the passage through the corridor. Of course, the soldiers had to be moved from these trenches so that they would be opened up, freed up for the passage of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for about how long was the period of cease-fire before the soldiers of the 28th Division began to pass through the open trenches?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between an hour or two hours, certainly, and it was agreed that it should go on for 24 hours; that is the same time on the next day, but it actually lasted longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go through a few documents with you relating to the events of that morning. Can we start with P254, please, a daily combat report of the Bratunac Brigade of the 15th of July. And under paragraph 2, we see it says: "Part of our forces has been sent to the area of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, 80 soldiers and another platoon has been sent to the Romanija Motorised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did that unit arrive and place itself under your command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now go to the duty operation officer's notebook P377, and we want page 141 in the English and B/C/S, of course; and Ms. Stewart, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, can you look at page 5759 and the entry ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Lazo says that everything is all right where he is -- the Bratunac people have arrived and are deployed at Parlog."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that the same unit we've just been looking at in the combat report of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is being referred to in the entry of 1230, the call from Zoran Jovanovic relating to 100 men and 130 for Maric?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, at 12.30, Zoran Jovanovic, that's Major Zoran Jovanovic who was the commander of a company which I said had been established previously and numbered 100 men, he -- and 130 men for Maric, food had to be delivered for them; and they were in the Crni Vrh area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look please at 7D774.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is an order of the Drina Corps dated the 16th of July of 1995 sent to the command of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the 1st Military Light Infantry Brigade and the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade: "Because of the very complex situation in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, this brigade must be reinforced so as to prevent enemy forces operating from the direction of Tuzla and enemy forces pulling out of Srebrenica via Kamenica towards Tuzla from linking up. "In order to assist the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, I hereby issue the following order: The command of 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade shall detach 100 men fit for active combat operations. "The command of the 1st Military Light Infantry Brigade shall directly contact the commander of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade to agree on coordinated action. "The command of the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade shall detach 30 men, and the command of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade shall receive soldiers from these units." Were they forces that on the 16th of July you anticipated arriving and being placed under your command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was expecting them, and as far as I can remember, the forces from the Bratunac Brigade did arrive and were deployed in the Crni Vrh area along the road together with R Battalion to the best of my recollection also a platoon from the Vlasenica Brigade arrived numbering 30 men; and the commander of the Milici Brigade contacted the commander of the Zvornik Brigade but did not arrive in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade with his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to come on quickly and deal with the self-propelled guns you were telling us about. Can we have a look at P1183 D, and it's under seal so it better not be broadcast. If it's an initial, I can't see anything offensive about the English translation. This is a conversation recorded at 7.06 in the morning of the 16th of July. You've obviously had the opportunity to read it, Mr. Pandurevic. To the best of your recollection, did you have a conversation like this and who with?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having a conversation with General Krstic about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you tell him about the taking of two self-propelled guns?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When asked by him about the situation, I reported to him that there was combat going on and that the Muslim forces had taken those two self-propelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now can we have a look at P2231, page 21, and P2232 page 19. This is the book of tactical intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There's an entry 238, "1140, Igman said that weapons are to be ready to fire at planned targets." In the book of codes or the list of codes for use on the 16th of July, who was Igman 1?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Igman was the name of the artillery battalion and Igman might have been a subordinate unit of that artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what does it appear has been listened into that Igman 1 has been saying about weapons being ready to fire at planned targets?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what's he talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand this conversation, I can't see the proper passages, the corresponding passages in the translation, but what this is about is that artillery has taken up its positions, selected its targets, and is ready to open fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, we'll have a break of 20 minutes in five minutes' time or earlier if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the bottom of that page. Palma in person; who's that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Palma in person was me, or rather the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Lovac 1 in person; who was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at all these documents and analysing them, I think it was Dragan Obrenovic; he was Lovac 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There may be an element of confusion here because the page in Serbian is not the right page. I think we need to go forward a page so that Mr. Pandurevic and all those who want to read it in that language can follow. Well it's further up the page, but I think it's too faint to read. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one more question on the first entry which presumably is now not on the page in Serbian. It says at 1140: "They seized some elements of our weapons but they did not fire because of the cease-fire." And it's reminded me that there is something I didn't ask you about. What happened after Obrenovic and his units had evacuated the command of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic then withdrew to the place where the 4th and 6th Battalions joined up. I continued negotiations and while the negotiations were going on, fire was not opened from artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened to the command of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Battalion also withdrew in the direction of Parlog where we later established a new command post for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did the forces of the 28th Division do after Obrenovic and the command of the 4th Battalion had withdrawn and whilst you were negotiating?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the 28th Division were already in the Baljkovica area along the road, that is a depression around the command post of the 4th Battalion and that was the axis along which they passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have a look, please, at P2231, B/C/S page 22 and English page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is Palma again to Lovac 1, so from what you tell us that's you talking to Obrenovic. We agreed that their axis is going to be towards the stream so that we liberate Breznik and Govedarice. What are they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a conversation in which I am informing Obrenovic what axis had been agreed for the passage of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it goes on: "We are going to open it there, and once it passes, we are returning to our old positions. It is about the withdrawal of our dead and wounded, and the Chetniks received an order to shoot if someone attempted to go into the depth of the territory. The Chetniks received an order not to open fire while the men were going through." How does that reflect your understanding of the agreement you reached with Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that's precisely what we agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, in military terms, was it necessary to open the corridor at Baljkovica for the forces of the 28th Division to pass to Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to open the corridor in order to save human lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your only military option?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not the only military option. From the military viewpoint, the purpose of fighting is to inflict losses on the enemy in terms of manpower, and this was an occasion to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What else could you have done other than open the corridor and let the forces of the 28th Division walk to Nezuk with their arms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could have betrayed the agreement I had made and when the 28th Division was concentrated in one place, in my sights, I could have fired on them from my weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we'll take a break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be of 20 minutes' duration starting from now, and there will be another break, short break at 5. I will communicate to you later anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions before we move on. During the making of the agreement on the 16th of July, can you recall now how many radio communications you had with Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After communication line was established, and after we started our conversation and negotiation about cease-fire and opening of corridor, we virtually never stopped our contact. We were in constant communication. This channel was open all the time, we were monitoring the development of the situation, and we reacted whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for how long did that contact continue?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in contact until nightfall, and that is when we talked about what arrangements to make for the night, and how things should go on during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did it go on after the 16th of July and, if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, I also talked with his division commander. I think his name was Salih Malkic, he was not, as far as I know, at the forward command post. And from him, I requested additional guarantees that during the night, their side with a would not undertake anything contrary to our agreement, and I was given that guarantee from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, probably my fault for asking a bad question, but what I meant was did you continue to have radio conversations with Muminovic after the 16th of July; and did they continue for a day, two days, what sort of period did you continue talking to him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the 17th of July, we were also in contact. On the 18th, we communicated a few times and after that, we spoke occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you spoke on the 18th and after that, what were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically remember an incident which took place on the 18th and which prompted me to contact him. There was a group of teenagers or rather men aged about 18 who were supposed to be escorted safely through our positions to Nezuk and handed over to Semso Muminovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we may come to that a little later on. Now, on an entirely different topic, during the course of your preparation of your case, have you had occasion to instruct a military expert witness?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military expert was present during the visits at the detention unit, and he was also present here during the breaks while he was listening the testimony of a prosecution witness. I discussed with him some general issues, and my overall instruction - if I may call it that - was for the expertise not to dwell on general principles only, but that it must go very much into the core of the problem and all the incidents that took place. I think I said that one should really get their shoes dirty rather than just walk on a pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well I'm really only dealing with one specific issue now which is the map you have behind you. Did you give instructions as to the drawing of that map?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so when we look at that map and the positioning of the forces, does that come from information that you gave to your military expert?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe that I was the only one who had a full insight into the engagement of all the forces at that time and in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I haven't mentioned it before, but the map that we've all been looking at is 7D1116. And it can be moved now. Now, throughout the course of the morning of the 16th of July, did you take the trouble to get in contact with General Krstic to see if it was okay for you to let the 28th Division go?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when I started negotiations about letting the 28th Division go through, I did not attempt to establish contact with anyone from the Superior Command. Therefore, during that period, I had no contact of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you not make contact with the Superior Command about what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted, in the spirit of the word that I gave to the other side, to see this agreement through to the end. I knew that I was not at the level of command that could do such a thing from the aspect of the combat rules and combat engagement rules, but I wanted to get this done and over with lest someone should prevent me from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have a look, please, at the duty officer's notebook, P377. Mr. Pandurevic, you're looking for page 766 and the rest of us, page 148. It's the last entry on that page which reads in English: "They called from Zlatar that the commander is to call the Zlatar duty officer or send a report --" I'm sorry, "or send a written report on the situation in the field at 1525 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Firstly, what was going on where you were at 1525 hours?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1525, the column of the 28th Division was already passing through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you at about half past 3.00 in the afternoon, or indeed at any time, made aware of this request for a report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was a request for me to either send a report or to call the duty officer at the corps or to send a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have a look at P1192. The B/C/S is under seal. And the B/C/S is C, the English B. This is an intercept of a radio communication a few minutes after the entry in the duty operations officer's notebook we've just been looking at, if the times are both accurate. And it is recorded as being someone from the Main Staff talking to somebody at Palma, and about halfway down the first page in English, the person from the Main Staff says: "You know what this is about. Have Vinko tell you what happened, and send it right away. Okay. So if there is no other, dictate what has been done and have him send it urgently, right away to the Main Staff, right away. Got it? Hello? Hello? "Yes. "Did you understand? Have Vinko dictate you -- well you have a wire line to him and send that urgently to us." In much the same vain. Now the entry we saw in the duty operation officer's notebook was from Zlatar, is that the Main Staff or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can go back to the beginning so that I can see who the speakers are. The one who was intercepting this conversation marked by X, someone from the Main Staff and by Y, the duty officer from the Zvornik Brigade. And this conversation was exactly about as you quoted, and it refers the events in Baljkovica in which I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware that -- well, I perhaps better get an answer to my first question. Zlatar is code for what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatar was the code-name for the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. And I think you told us that when you looked at the entry in the duty operation officer's notebook, that you became aware that the Drina Corps wanted an explanation. Did you become aware that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska wanted an explanation as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the reason for the Drina Corps to request this information was their need to pass it on to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Can we look now, please, at P1194 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's something that may want to be cleared up in the question there's a suggestion that the General actually read this in the duty officer notebook. It's a little unclear whether he's just now read it or read it in the preparation of his case or read it at the time. You may want to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, we're looking at certain, as it were, extraneous documents to what was going on where you were. And we looked, first of all, at an entry in the duty officer's notebook which was timed at 1525. And really the question to you is: If you became aware that the Drina Corps wanted a report from you and, if so, approximately when did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Zlatar or rather the Drina Corps was requesting a report from the duty officer Palma, he was obliged to pass this request immediately to me, to my command post and instruct me to send a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the question, really, is did you know that? Did you know that they were contacting the command of the Zvornik Brigade down in Zvornik while you were up at Delici?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer from the command in Zvornik passed Zlatar's request or the Drina Corps' request to me which means that somebody from the Drina Corps spoke to him. Nobody spoke directly to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that answers the question. But did you also become aware that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska were contacting the duty officer at Zvornik directly themselves asking for the same thing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know at that moment who the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade was talking to, but I knew what he was talking about because he requested a report from me, and I knew at the time that a report was requested by both the corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on to P1194 A, about half an hour later. The B/C/S is B, and I don't think it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Here, an intercept of a conversation between Zlatar and Palma at 1602: "Give me 01." Who would 01 be at Palma?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody wants to speak to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who would Zlatar 01 be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It says that the Palma, presumably duty officer, says they're not able to reach the commander. Can you offer any explanation why General Krstic should be told that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer Palma said that they were unable to get in touch or rather reach the commander, that was me. In any case, they were able to contact me because everybody knew where I was. But at that point, I didn't want to take any call coming from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we move on, please, to P1195 C, about 10 or 15 minutes after the last call. The passage in B/C/S is at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At 1615, we recorded a conversation between the duty officer at the Main Staff and General Mladic, and we could not hear. The conversation was as follows: "Good day, General, sir. Well I just sent the telegram to Toso. The President called a short while ago. He said he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic has arranged passage for the Muslims over to the territory. Since I have no communication with him, I asked the duty officer urgently to connect me with him to have him send me a telegram with that information and not to do anything without authorisation until he receives our answer. Now I'm waiting for them to call me because Pandurevic hasn't called for the last four ... "Yes, of course. No, but there are both fighters and civilians. "Nobody is playing around. That's just the information we got. I spoke to Krsto down there. He says it's going well ..." And the latter part provisions are irrelevant. Do you know who Karisik is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karisik was, as far as I knew, Milenko Karisik was at the time chief of the public security at the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. On that day, he was in the Baljkovica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you become aware on the afternoon of the 16th of July that the president and General Mladic were interested in what was going on at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn about that on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Can we go back to the duty officer's notebook, please, P377. For you, Mr. Pandurevic, page 767, and for the rest of us page 149. We'll kill two birds with one stone and look at the entries for both 1620 and 1640. So 5 and 20 minutes after the last intercept respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At 1620 hours: "Message from Zlatar that one officer from the command was to go immediately to the commander and send a written report on the current situation. The agreement and arrangements made with the other side immediately sent to Mijatovic." Do you recall whether you saw Mijatovic at any time during the afternoon of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably the last effort on the part of the corps command to contact me, and that is why they requested an officer to be sent from the brigade command to establish direct contact with me. Therefore, Mr. Mijatovic was sent out. As far as I recall, he did come to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The second message from entry: "Message from Zlatar that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640. The message through the 1st Battalion that Popovic must report to the duty officer so he can be sent on a task by Zlatar." Did you see Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic at any stage during the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to page 767. And that's page 149 for the rest of us. Yes I'm sorry it's the next entry at 1705: "Thirty soldiers came from Vlasenica and were sent immediately to the IKM at Gnovice [phoen] as ordered. Zlatar was immediately informed, and Zlatar asked again whether the report had come from the commander." What did Mr. Mijatovic do, if you remember, when he came.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he told me that I had to send a written report to the corps command about everything that took place that day. I don't think that he stayed long, and then he went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that brings us to a little after 5.00. Did you accept that you would have to tell your superior command what you'd done at some stage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I realised that I would have to send this report. I had no option after so many interventions. Probably I would have sent this report at the time that I usually did even if there hadn't been so much pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what had you been doing between 11.00 that morning and 5.00 in the afternoon when we see the last entry here in the duty officer's notebook that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, I was supervising the passage of the 28th Division. I maintained contact with Semso Muminovic, and then at around 1700 hours, I dictated a report to Captain Milisav Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we come now, please, to P330, the regular combat report for the 16th of July. And just so we can put this into the careful chronology we've been building, Mr. Pandurevic, can we have a look at page 2 first. Sorry, page 2 in English but not in B/C/S. All we want to do in B/C/S is go to the bottom of the page and look to the record of the sending of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, there's a number there, Mr. Pandurevic, 1158. What does that denote?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see in front of me is an interim combat report relating to the 16th. As far as I understood you, you made reference to a regular report. The number you are asking me about is the number of the telegram or rather the report under which it was registered at the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where is the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications centre was at the command in Standard, the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just quickly tell us how this report came to be sent by you? What was the processes -- what were the processes involved, as it were, in delivering it to Standard to be sent?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were only a few reports that I personally dictated, those were the reports dealing with a very complex situation and this is one of such reports. This interim combat report dated the 16th, I personally dictated as I said to Captain Milisav Petrovic, and thereafter this report was carried by a courier who was driven to the communications centre. After encrypting it, the communications centre passed it on to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from the stamp at the bottom, and the handwritten additions to the document, what can we tell about the history of the transmission of this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signalsman, when he received the document in writing, he typed in the contents into the encryption teleprinting machine and tried to send it through the radio relay connection to the corps. Here we see his note saying that due to poor, or rather due to a bad relay line, the telegram was repeated several times. So it was ready to go at 1810, but it was not actually sent before 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just briefly want to have a look at another document before we come back to this and that is 7D532, the regular combat report for the 16th of July. Again, can we look at the end of the document which I think is page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, this document has a number. What number does this document have?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has the number 1159, so it's the next document after 1158.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But what can we glean from the box as to the sequence in which this was sent in relation to the last document in your regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signalsman first received the previous telegram which was the interim combat report and entered it under number 1158. Then he received the regular combat report and entered it under the following number, the next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But the transmission of this report, when was it successfully transmitted, the regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This regular combat report was sent off at 11.20. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather 1820, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why, for technical reason, this one did go through at that time and the other one didn't. It's possible that he sent the report thinking that it would be received in the corps but that it wasn't received; and then later on, there was a bad line, and there was several attempts to send the report again. I'm not a signalsman. I'm not a technician by profession, so I really can't offer any other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I would like, Mr. Pandurevic, to see the bottom right part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm trying not to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We see RPT 1830, which is similar to something we saw written on the other document. Even though you're not a signalsman, what does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't see this before. Probably this one also went at 1830. RPT, I don't know if it was RTP I would understand it as a radio teleprinter, but I'm unable to explain the meaning of the abbreviation RPT.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. But what you can tell us is what you had to do with the writing of the regular combat report of the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regular combat report was written by the duty operations officer. He sent off that report before my handwritten signature so you can see just the typed version of my name, and in this regular combat report, there is very little information about what was really going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I will lead if nobody minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If RPT indicates, as it were, the time at which the document was successfully sent, it looks as if the regular combat report arrived first by about a couple of hours. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's evident from what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So can we have a look at paragraph 1 of the regular combat report that was received by the Drina Corps: "The enemy deployed large forces in front of the forward line of our defence, with which from early morning, they launched a very heavy artillery-infantry attack on the area of the 7th, 4th, and 6th Infantry Battalions along the Parlog-Baljkovica-Rijeka-Pandurica axis, in conjunction with the forces which had pulled out from Srebrenica. They are trying to penetrate our defence lines and create conditions to pull out a large number of armed soldiers and civilians from the Kamenica area via Crni Vrh, Cetino Brdo and Baljkovica. Their intention is to link up with the 2nd Corps. Fighting is still going on, and we will send more detailed information in an interim report." Do you know who actually wrote that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the initials I have seen at the bottom of the document, according to the rules of office correspondence, the initials are MT; and I think they refer to Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as at about 6.00 in the evening of the 16th of July, how accurately did what he told corps command reflect what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not reflect the situation accurately because at that time in the evening, there was no combat going on. The column of the 28th Division was then passing through without any hindrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you relay information from the forward command post back to the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade as to what was actually going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not relay anything to him. He was receiving brief telegrams from the battalion commands as to what had happened in the course of the day and based on that, he compiled this report. Whether he obtained any information in some other way, I don't know. I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So you don't know why his report is so inaccurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at your report, P330: "As of 0400 hours, the enemy has continued intensive attacks on the brigade area along the entire front line with particular intensity in the defence areas of the 7th, 4th, 6th and 3rd Infantry Battalions." How accurately did that reflect the events of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not fully reflect the events that took place that morning. The attack began at 0400 hours but did not continue. There was no previous attack. The attack was not along the entire front line, so it was not this whole line that was attacked from the north to the south-west. Rather, it was the areas of the 7th, the 4th and the 6th Battalions, their areas of defence that had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Using all their forces, the 24th and 25th Infantry Division and Bosnian Army 2nd Corps Intervention Units fired almost a thousand projectiles of varying calibre." How accurately did that reflect what had happened on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that in front of the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade was the 24th Division, not the entire division. Its command was in Zivinice, and the axis of attack and the width of the front of the attack had the capacity of one brigade not two divisions. So the 25th Division was not engaged in combat activities in the attack on the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Parts of the Srebrenica 28th Infantry Battalion together with previously-infiltrated groups carried out a synchronised kamikaze attack against the 4th Battalion, our positions, weapons, and other equipment." How accurately does that reflect what happened on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had not been any previously infiltrated group from the direction of the 2nd Corps, there was only what I previously spoke about when the self-propelled weapons were taken, so this is partly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Kamikaze attack?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we all know what a kamikaze means. It's a term from World War II. I tried to describe in what way they had taken those self-propelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Using their numerical advantage, they surrounded the 4th Battalion, counting soldiers and civilians armed and unarmed, altogether about 7.000." How accurate is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the 4th Battalion could not have been surrounded because it is -- it was at the front line, that's this part here. And in terms of numbers, this number is more than double the one of the previously day. I wasn't sure how many men there were, but when observing the passage of the column, I thought there were between 4.000 and 5.000 or 6.000. It's very hard to estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll pass over the self-propelled guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "By continuous pressure from the front, they managed to seize three of our trenches in the Poljana area and link up part of their forces with the others in the wider area of Baljkovica." Was that an accurate reflection of what happened on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't manage to take these three trenches as you see in point 2 where it says: "We have managed to repel all the attacks from the front line."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were there any trenches in particular you were referring to in that paragraph of this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the forward defence line. We repelled all attacks, and these three trenches are mentioned because these were the trenches that we ourselves freed up in order to enable the passage of the 28th Division column.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "The brigade's problem is that a part of our forces is surrounded in the Baljkovica area." Was that an accurate reflection of what had happened on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the forces from Baljkovica, we pulled them out of the area of the command post before the 28th Division column arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 3: "In view of the great pressure on the brigade's area of responsibility, the losses sustained, the inability of the surrounded forces to hold out for long, the abandonment of the Zvornik command to deal as best it could with the Srebrenica Turks and served it right when it was the brigade that forced them out of Srebrenica into its own area, coupled with the absolute determination of the Turks to save at least some lives regardless of loss --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. The last word I see translated is "lives." " ... regardless of losses, and in order to prevent losses in our own ranks, I have decided in view of the situation to open a corridor along the line of the three lost trenches, for the civilian population, about 5.000 of them. I have agreed on a method of evacuation with the enemy side and this is now going forward."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How does that reflect the agreement you had reached?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that they should all pass through together, armed men, unarmed men, and civilians. So what it says here is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "I have requested the release of a captured policeman and my own missing soldiers. This procedure is in progress, and I think I will succeed. It is likely that a certain number of soldiers got out among the civilians but all who passed, pass through unarmed." How does that reflect the reality of the situation on the ground at the time you were writing this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not reflect the reality of the situation on the ground. As I said, they were all passing through. This is my personal attempt to protect myself because of my responsibility for what I had decided to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you've probably answered this question, but let me put it at the end of that. Why did you portray the combat situation in the way that you did in paragraph 1 of this report to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described it in such a way that I could represent to the corps command through the report that the situation was more dramatic and more grave than it really was, hoping that they would understand my actions in putting a stop to the fighting and opening up the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you represent the agreement you had reached in the way that you did in paragraph 3 of this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was all contrary to the orders that I had which I had received on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have to ask you about two particular sentences, Mr. Pandurevic. The sentence in brackets, four lines into paragraph 3: "And served it right when it was the brigade that forced them out of Srebrenica into its own area:" Why did you dictate that to Milisav Petrovic at the forward command post on the afternoon of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interim combat report could not have been written in this way by anyone except me. I put these words in brackets remembering well the 11th of July and the meeting in the command of the Bratunac Brigade when I was very roughly interrupted when putting forward my proposals as to how to treat the 28th Division. Within the scope of the Krivaja 95 Operation, I had been given the most difficult axis of attack. I had moved the 28th Division from its area of defence and the military action that would most logically follow after all this under the rules would be to pursue the enemy, to get on to the enemy's back, to attack their flanks, to set up ambushes, to set out to destroy the enemy. I felt that the 28th Division had moved from its area of defence under the pressure of Tactical Group 1; and when I said that we ourselves pushed them there, that's what I was referring to because if I hadn't set them in motion, they wouldn't have been there, and I would not have had this problem with them. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you would just speak the words inside those brackets for us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well that's what they deserve. They themselves pushed them from Srebrenica to their area." I was referring to the Zvornik Brigade, referring to myself, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, the last sentence of the report. Paragraph 6: "I consider that the Krivaja 95 Operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I don't know how to find the right word. It's a slap on the wrist for the command because the aim of Krivaja 95 was to separate the enclaves and prevent communication of enemy soldiers behind our front lines. Later on, the aim of the operation was changed. Further operations were undertaken and what did we get? We got large groups of the 28th Division, a great many of them, in the rear of our forces. Among them, a certain number of civilians, and this kind of situation did not suit anyone, either the Muslims or the Serbs. That's why I thought that all this had to be brought to an end in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of mood were you in when you sat down to dictate this report to Milisav Petrovic on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work I was doing at that time was very important to me. I made a decision on my own initiative. I opened up the front line. I trusted the enemy. Quite the opposite might have happened. Through that open corridor, they could have pumped in the forces of the 2nd Corps and I could have been faced with total ruin. That's what I was concerned about. Another reason for my concern was the many requests for me to send a report as soon as possible. I found this irritating, and that's why I compiled it in this way. I thought, Well, if that's what you want, here's your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you wish, Mr. Haynes, we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That is actually a very good moment, but I obviously misunderstood what you said earlier on. I thought we were doing two longer sessions, but we can break now. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't want to unduly presurise your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no. It's strange because I had a conversation with Ms. Stewart in the last break trying to work out when the next one will be, but now that you've told me when it is, I'm more than happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also I had some problems that I had to look into as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before break, can I ask one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, in your previous answer, I wanted to just clear. In the course of your answer that you said, "Later on, the aim of the operation was changed." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain in detailed terms what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was the 9th of July when the document reached the IKM of the corps at Pribicevac saying that the president of the republic was satisfied with the progress of the operation, and that he approved the continuation of the operation and the VRS to enter Srebrenica. That is what I meant, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
