utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, with your indulgence, we'll leave approximately five minutes or so before the end so that we hear some submissions on the an urgent motion that has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Lovely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About five minutes, I understand, would be sufficient. Or more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mentioned that I would maybe need five minutes but that was just me and it's not my motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's only you that we are going to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The rest has been put in writing, already. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll leave ten to be to the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were just describing to us the dictation of the irregular combat report of the 16th of July at the IKM, and I know you've already told us, but so far as you can work out, about what time of day did you do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been at around 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you, by that time of that day, seen Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't met him personally by that time on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what had he been up to since you spoke to him about the soldier Salikovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole time, he was engaged in combat operations in the area around the command of the 4th Battalion and then upon cessation of combat, he pulled out at the linking of the 4th and 6th Battalions; he inspected the positions in the area and supervised the activities of the 2nd Corps or rather monitored the activities of the 2nd Corps, and the activities of our forces in the area where the 2nd Corps was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did he do that from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did that directly from the positions of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first see him on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him to come over to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he come alone or did he come with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Milan Jolovic aka "Legenda" was with him and possibly a soldier courier, but I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In the presence of others or on your own?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we discussed the situation on the ground, specifically the development that took place by that time. I gave tasks to Jolovic aka "Legenda" to take direct control with his forces over the night of the corridor and the front line. And after that, I had a private conversation with Jolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have a private conversation with "Legenda" or Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were both there, we discussed the overall situation of the day, and I issued tasks to "Legenda." He left and Obrenovic stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Pandurevic, I was just trying to correct something in the transcript. The private conversation you had after "Legenda" had left, who was that with?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did the conversation begin?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It began with my question about what information he had about POWs in the area of Zvornik relating to the information that I received in the course of the day from Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did Obrenovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He started telling me his story and informing me about what, according to him, he knew at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he tell you what schools he knew about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, but I'm not sure it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once you mention schools that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is classic. What did he tell you? I mean this is inexcusable in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Haynes knows it, but anyway, the witness has heard everything in any case now. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did he know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is -- I don't even know what the proper -- that -- how does he know what Obrenovic knows? I mean that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Can't you reconcile yourself with the suggestion made by Mr. McCloskey himself, what did he tell you? I mean it's the simplest and harmless way of approaching the subject, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure. I'm not sure he even needs the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Tell us about the conversation, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I told you that Brano Grujic had informed me about prisoners of war being in schools in Petkovci and Pilici, I asked him what he knew about that. He then started telling me his story if I may continue and tell you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obrenovic told me that on the evening of the 13th, Drago Nikolic passed on information to him that he had received from the security organ that pursuant to the order of the Main Staff of the VRS, a number of prisoners were to be transferred to the area of Zvornik. And that a triage was going to be carried out, or a screening. Those who were suspected of committing war crimes would be sent to Batkovic and the rest of them would be exchanged. He also told him - I mean Drago Nikolic - that his obligation was to wait for the arrival of these prisoners, that these prisoners would come under escort and with security guards, but that he needed Obrenovic to place at his disposal a number of policemen for any eventuality. Obrenovic, according to his statement, acted accordingly. He placed Jasikovac and another five or six policemen at his disposal. Then he spoke about his being most of the time in the field setting up ambushes for the 28th Division, and that he just went to the command occasionally. What is particularly interesting is that he told me a story relating to events that took place on the evening of the 14th. He told me that on the evening of the 14th, or, rather, during the night, he sent an interim combat report to the corps command asking for reinforcement given that he had estimated the forces of the 28th Division, the size of them, as that he needed reinforcement. He spoke to Dragan Jokic on that occasion who was duty operations officer and who told him, according to his words, that Colonel Beara had been in the command with some other men unknown to him. That from representatives of the authorities, they had requested certain machinery to bury the people who were shot dead in Orahovac. They also asked -- they actually asked the machinery to be provided by companies; but after they had been told that some of the machines were mobilised by the engineer company of the Zvornik Brigade, they took one of the machines from Glinica or the company called Birac Holding, one machine from the Josanica quarry and another machine from the Josanica company. These machines were used to bury the people killed in Orahovac. Jokic told him that he couldn't do anything about that. I asked Obrenovic whether he informed about this or did he pass this information to anyone; but he said that in view of the information that he had received from Drago Nikolic, these men were to arrive pursuant to an order from the Main Staff and that he considered that this should not be passed on to anyone as information. I also asked him if he knew if any member of the Zvornik Brigade took part in these activities in Orahovac. He answered that apart from being contacted by Nikolic, to whom he gave the men in question, he had no information about anyone from the Zvornik Brigade including Drago Nikolic took part in the executions. This is his story relating to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he only know about Orahovac or did he know about some other site?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Same objection. He can't get into what he knew. That's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he tell you only about Orahovac, or did he tell you about some other site?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. What did he tell you? Did he tell you anything else? He cannot put in the answers or part of the answers. He knows that. It's been mercifully quiet over here for the last several days. He knows how to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A leading question is one which suggests the answer. That does not suggest an answer. If you ask somebody: Where were you? That is not a leading question. If you ask somebody: Were you here or there? That is not a leading question. If you say to somebody: You were not there, were you? That is a leading question. That is not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are getting into niceties, legal niceties on what is and what is not a leading question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in the presence of the witness who we have agreed has a right to be present during these discussions. So you either move on or you rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What else did you tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also told me that on the 16th, while he was with the 6th Battalion, he met Ostoja Stanisic, the commander of the 6th Battalion, who told him that prisoners had been in the school in Petkovci and that according to his deputy's report, Majo Milosevic or Marko Milosevic, execution of these men was carried out at the Crveni Mulj dam; and that some of them were killed in the vicinity of the school itself. He also told me that Ostoja didn't mention it or rather told him that no member of the 6th Battalion took part in these executions but that some men, some dead men were collected around the school and driven to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did this conversation last?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour, 45 minutes. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you do as a result of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this had been the topic of conversation for three years, and someone might find it easy to talk about it, at that moment, this information was shocking to me. I simply couldn't believe that something like that could have happened. I asked him if he knew about any similar things. He said he didn't. And I decided to send him that evening to Zvornik to the duty operations officer at the command or to the security organ and try to find out additional information about prisoners in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we clarify this. When you said at the start of your last answer, "Since this has or had been the topic of conversation for three years, someone might find it easy to talk about," which three years did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the years of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you were telling us about your reaction at the time you were talking to Obrenovic, did you say you simply believed that or you simply could not believe that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to believe something like that at a time like that. I cooperated with Obrenovic during the war. I had experience, and I thought that he wouldn't tell me such things if they were found groundless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time did he leave the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps at around 1900 hours. I'm not sure. He had some other things to see to, then he had to go to the command, then he wanted to go home to spend the night and return to the IKM in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what arrangement did you make with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him to check things and to collect as much information as he could about the POWs, and whether there was any other school or any other location where these men were being kept, and whether they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we just take a little time, as it were, tracking the movements of the two of you. And we'll have a look, please, at the duty officer's notebook. Mr. Pandurevic, for you, page 769. For the rest of us, page 151 and that's P377. And I want to direct your attention really to three entries on this page. Firstly, the top one: "At 1830, a unit from the 16th Krajina Brigade arrived from Banja Luka. The commander at the IKM and the commander of the unit were informed." Can you tell us what that refers to and whether you can recall that event?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this refers to a company that had been sent from the 6th Krajina Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps to assist the Zvornik Brigade. This is the time when it arrived in the general area of Orahovac, and I was informed about that because at the time, I was at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you and who is referred to there by the title "the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This probably refers to the man who commanded this unit although I know this is a bit illogical. I know this was a major and operations officer who came as an advanced party from the brigade, and the company was following him so this probably refers to this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall what his name was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Dragicevic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go down the page where we see an entry saying: "Men from Bratunac are in Orahovac. Obrenovic asked the commander what to do with them at 1920 hours." Who are the men from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the men who had been sent in compliance with General Krstic's order on the 16th as additional assistance to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, on the previous page, last line, line 25, the -- your client mentions 16th Krajina Brigade, which corps did it form part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was part of the 1st Krajina Corps, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one under Momir Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why, at 20 past 7.00 in the evening of the 16th of July was Obrenovic asking what to do with the men from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I sent him from the IKM to meet this company coming from Banja Luka, this is where he found the men from Bratunac about whom we had no information that they would arrive. They did arrive actually and that is why he was asking what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where was he when he was asking you that question?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably asked this question of the duty operations officer, he probably called him from Orahovac, Orahovac or some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's move down. At 1940 hours, the men from Krajina went with Chief Obrenovic to search the terrain." We can probably work out who the men from Krajina are, but you tell us.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the men from the company that we have just mentioned, Obrenovic met up with them. He was about to inform them about the terrain, show them the features where they would be carrying out their tasks, and he probably directed them to the next area in order to search the ground. As far as I can remember, it lasted for a short period of time, and then they went back to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where would he have met up with them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at P1202, B in the B/C/S and C in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A short transcript of a intercepted radio communication involving Colonel Cerovic and the Palma duty officer, apparently, at 2126 on the 16th of July: "Colonel Cerovic was informed that at 2100, 30 men came from Badem; at 1705 hours, 30 men came from Dobos; and at 1725 hours, 100 men came from Banja Luka. General Mladic asked through Colonel Cerovic what had happened to three self-propelled guns, and at 2135 hours, the duty officer informed him that the guns were on the Serbian side." Do you have a recollection of this, as it were, inquiry?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand this, Cerovic was looking for the confirmation of the information that General Krstic's order had been carried out in terms of sending soldiers from Bratunac, i.e., Badem and Vlasenica, i.e., Dobos; and he also took this opportunity to inquire about the self-propelled guns. I don't remember receiving this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well let's move back to the duty officer's notebook please, page 771 for you, please, Mr. Pandurevic; and for the rest of us page 153. The bottom of the page: "The security centre reported at 2317 hours that enemy groups have been spotted moving from Kusonja to Crni Vrh. Passed on to the commander at the brigade IKM." Did you receive information of that sort at about 2317 on the evening of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the IKM at the time and this information arrived from Zvornik and obviously they deemed important enough to pass it on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what happened at nightfall with the passing of the column?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was the passage of the column would be suspended at nightfall, and that everything would remain in place as it was, that nobody would move, and we would continue in the same way the next morning. As I already said, that is why I talked to the commander of the 24th Division, Salih Malkic asking him for additional confirmation that they would honour the agreement. The night went by peacefully, and I spent it in a make-shift facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Delici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have omitted to ask you this question before, and I'll do so at this moment: Did you see the column passing through the vacated trenches?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was observing the column on the 16th and the 17th as it was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what could you observe?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that the -- that there were quite a few people in the column, different people. Some of them were wearing uniforms, some were wearing civilian clothes, some were armed, some were unarmed, some had a rifle, some had walking sticks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you able to give us your estimation as to how many people passed through the three trenches?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say at least 5.000 or 6.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what effect did their passing have on the environment, on the ground they passed over?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think whether they left some traces while passing by, yes, they did, although it was summertime. And the vegetation was lush. The grass was high. The path that the column pass the down was completely devoid the grass. It was totally trodden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to pop to a couple of entries in the small hours in the duty officer's notebook. Can we go to page 773 where you are, Mr. Pandurevic, and page 155 for the rest of us. The entry at 5.10 in the morning: "Milenko Jovanovic to send food and soft drinks to the IKM. The IKM called. Milenko Jovanovic was informed." What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Jovanovic was the commander of the staff command in the Zvornik Brigade, and this was a message sent at my request that certain foodstuffs and soft drinks should be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly, can we go to page 772 in your book, and page 154 for the rest of us. We see there -- well, perhaps you can go back a page to page 771 to see if we can get some idea of when these entries were written. What's the last entry on the previous page, in terms of a time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's 2330.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we now go back -- forward to page 772, what's the first, as it were, timed entry we can see on that page?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the first part of the text, and it says 2340.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The entry at 4.30 -- I'm sorry: "At 2340 hours, Obrenovic reported that there is a tank up there to be assigned and that Manco is going and with manpower and that armoured equipment is given to the Commander Jovanovic and disband his company and that all of them should report to their units. "At 4.30 to come and pick up Obrenovic at his home; wake him up. Petrovic does not have to come -- "

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry: "Petrovic does not have to come for Obrenovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who is Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original, it says at 4.30. He should come to pick up Obrenovic at his home; wake him up. And Petrovic doesn't have to come to pick up Obrenovic. I think this is Milisav Petrovic. As I remember, he was Dragan Obrenovic's kum. And in the brigade, of course, he was the chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did Dragan Obrenovic spend the night of the 16th and 17th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spent it at home, at his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll stop there for tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. We will continue with your testimony on Monday. In the meantime, we received today a joint motion of which you are aware. Basically requesting the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to proceed with its cross-examination of co-accused Pandurevic before the joint defence, before the defence teams. Are you in a position to reply orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I apologise, I have -- I heard about this this afternoon when Mr. Bourgon informed me that he would be sending me a motion. I had spoken to Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic, I think, the day before when they requested this of me and I said, No, I would like to go with the set-up that we've been going on all along. This motion I received at 1.22 this afternoon, and, obviously, I've been in trial with all of us for most of that afternoon. Having said that, in looking over this, there is no law cited for this proposition at all, really, except the -- in the fairness of them to be able to put on their case. You have set out, well years ago, I'm not sure it's three years, but it was a long time ago, perhaps it was three years, the rules by which we would be doing this; and those are the rules we've been relying on, and we've been following, and we don't see any reason to change them at this point. The Defence says in paragraph 10 that: "Moreover, for the other co-accused to be able to assess whether the testimony of co-accused on the stand affects their respective defences, it is necessary that the Prosecution's case against this co-accused be known to them." Well, the Prosecution's case, I believe they're speaking of General Pandurevic, has been made for these last many years in the indictment, in the trial brief, in the opening statements, and all the evidence. I think we have a very good idea from even the testimony as it's come out that the Defence clearly understands what the case is against them. And so I think what they really want to know is what, based on the General's testimony, how will his testimony affect the case against their clients? And they would rather see me cross-examine him first to see what he says on that so they can do it afterward. That's not the way it's been designed. There's no reason for that. And the Prosecution, if we switch this, will be left with a situation where I cross-examine, and then all the accused will have the ability, with leading questions, to take the General through their case as they please. From what it appears thus far, that may be very valuable for them to do that, from what I see from where I see the General coming from. And then I'm left with no ability to cross-examine the General. It shouldn't work that way. They need to make their strategic decision now -- well, after, when the General's testifying. We're only halfway through. There's a lot more to be said. I think it's going to be much clearer. The answers that they want answers to will be much more clear to them once the General is through, the things that they're concerned about, I have no doubt by the detail that we're going through they're going to see some of the answers. So there's no reason to do this. There's no prejudice to them strategically, yes, they'd be better off that way, but this is not what this is about. And frankly, if, during my cross-examination, something new and different and rather exculpatory to one of the accused comes out, I will probably not be objecting to Defence counsel who that is affected by that to be able to put questions to the General on that particular point. I don't want to leave any accused hanging out to dry, so to speak, and having them not be able to respond. But this idea that this is going to save some time is just not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes, where do we -- how is it going? Where do you stand? How many more hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I've changed headphone sets. To have estimated 30 hours and be on schedule to do it in 30 hours, I pat myself on the back for frankly because I think that's pretty much exactly what it's going to be. The amount of material we are getting through we can gauge -- we can project quite accurately now, I think I will take a couple or maybe three days of next week. And that will be eight or nine days which is 30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's been 19 hours. You've been 19 hours so far so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I knew somebody would be timing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we're talking about another 11, 12 hours. Okay. Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be thinking about this matter, and we will come down with our decision on Monday orally. In the meantime, I wouldn't suggest that anyone takes risks and assume the decision to go one way or another. So be prepared just in case. Thank you. We will resume on Monday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just ask you one thing. Due to the lateness of this, if there is a particular question you have regarding this motion, I -- if you could ask us to address it because there's a lot of points in here, and I did not want to hold us up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. If I may say so, this is a matter that we preferred not to discuss amongst ourselves once we were told that you would be responding orally today. So we prefer to wait, hear your submissions, and I think in the few minutes that we have left, it will be not exactly the right thing to do on our part to rush into a decision. We need to discuss. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of February, 2009 at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.15 p.m.,
